A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AVA-VLA work. All 18 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v3, including appendices, support comparison. Text, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original AVA-VLA experiments on LIBERO, CALVIN, LIBERO+, and Mobile ALOHA, including benchmark results, component ablations, and token-pruning analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation and real-robot results and adds matched-training comparisons, regularizer and CALVIN component ablations, and qualitative failure cases.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 and Appendix A retain the recurrent-state construction, state-based action initialization, AVA architecture, attention reweighting, training losses, and inference procedure. The additional experiments test existing components and alternative training conditions without revising the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four LIBERO suites, CALVIN ABC-to-D setting, seven LIBERO+ perturbation dimensions, and four Mobile ALOHA tasks. The new ablations and failure cases use this existing coverage rather than introducing another dataset, domain, or test scenario.

E2.justification: v3 adds VLA-Adapter to the CALVIN comparison in Table 2, reporting an average completed length of 4.42. The existing benchmark and real-robot comparator sets otherwise remain intact. Newly discussed methods such as MemoryVLA are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New Table 7 introduces a controlled LIBERO comparison: both methods start from the same pretrained OpenVLA checkpoint and train for 100,000 steps with batch size 256. This supplements the retained main recipe, which initializes AVA-VLA from trained OpenVLA-OFT and fine-tunes for 40,000 steps with batch size 64. Existing task splits, metrics, and real-robot trial counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of the extra-training confound (Table 7), the attention regularizer (Table 8 and Figure 12), component contributions on CALVIN (Table 9), and manipulation failures (Figure 13). These substantially expand the questions investigated. The LIBERO+ robustness study and earlier attention visualizations are retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both use point estimates, and the stated real-robot trial counts are unchanged. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises AVA-VLA's per-suite-policy Goal score from 98.2% to 97.9% and its average from 98.3% to 98.2%. Table 2 revises OpenVLA-OFT's CALVIN average from 4.10 to 4.28; AVA-VLA remains at 4.65. New results include 98.3% versus 96.8% under matched training, 97.5% without the regularizer versus 98.0% with it, and CALVIN component-only averages of 4.63 and 4.61. These additions substantially expand the findings; the matched-training result is not a same-setting improvement over the earlier main experiment.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, recurrent-state definition, attention equations, and loss definitions in Equations 1–14 remain substantively unchanged. Notational corrections and expanded explanations introduce no new assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same core contributions: POMDP-inspired recurrent conditioning, active visual attention, strong benchmark performance, and transfer to real-world manipulation. The new supporting experiments do not redefine these claims or their scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning architectural benefits versus additional training, complementary component roles across task horizons, and the regularizer's role in suppressing distracting attention. New Appendix E attributes precision-sensitive failures to accumulated perception errors and belief drift, connects this limitation to long-horizon pruning sensitivity, and discusses possible remedies. v1 lacks this explicit limitations analysis.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a project-page link, reports that the added modules contain fewer than 50 million parameters and under 1% of the full model, and documents the new matched-training settings. The existing architecture descriptions, hardware, principal hyperparameters, and real-robot implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: New Appendix C substantially expands positioning beyond v1's general VLA and sequential-VLM discussion. It distinguishes AVA-VLA from MemoryVLA's explicit memory retrieval and discusses its relationship to VLN-BERT, SafeVLA, NaVid, and recurrent reinforcement-learning approaches. These are substantive comparisons concerning memory representation and visual processing, alongside additional citations such as VLA-Adapter.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion are rewritten, introductory and technical prose is polished, and explanations of component roles are expanded. The supplement gains dedicated discussion and limitations sections, while execution trajectories move into Appendix B. The main five-section narrative and most technical exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The manuscript changes from a predominantly single-column preprint layout to a two-column layout, with extensive table and figure resizing and relocation. v1 Figure 4 becomes supplementary Figure 6, and the existing attention figures are redistributed. v3 also adds Tables 7–9, a robot-platform image, regularizer visualization, and failure-case panels, and expands several captions.

improvement.justification: v1's main training recipe leaves additional training as a plausible explanation for AVA-VLA's advantage. v3 substantially strengthens attribution through the common-initialization, matched-budget comparison in Table 7. The regularizer and CALVIN ablations test previously underexamined design choices, while failure cases and explicit limitations provide a more balanced account of applicability. These gains materially improve empirical support and transparency despite unchanged uncertainty reporting and unexplained revisions to some existing scores.
